## Estimate a mean

The package calculates intervals for the ordinary population mean. This example
uses independent normal observations with known population mean 2.

```{r}
library(bambaganaCI)
set.seed(1998)
x <- rnorm(30, mean = 2, sd = 1)
standard <- mean_t_ci(x)
set.seed(1998)
bootstrap <- bootstrap_mean_ci(x, B = 2000)
standard
bootstrap
```

The standard t interval has exact coverage under the independent normal model
with common positive variance. Bootstrap coverage depends on the population,
sample size, interval method, and resampling accuracy.

## Extract results

```{r}
coef(bootstrap)
confint(bootstrap)
rbind(as.data.frame(standard), as.data.frame(bootstrap))
bootstrap$diagnostics
```

`confint()` extracts the stored interval. To request a different confidence level,
recalculate using `conf`; it cannot simply relabel the existing interval.

```{r}
set.seed(1998)
interval_90 <- bootstrap_mean_ci(x, conf = 0.90)
confint(interval_90)
```

The `$estimate`, `$lower`, `$upper`, and `$bootstrap_means` fields remain available
for existing code. Bootstrap SE is the standard deviation of the resampled means;
it is not the standard deviation of the original observations.

## Compare supported methods on one sample

```{r}
methods <- c("percentile", "basic", "normal", "bca")
comparison <- lapply(methods, function(method) {
  set.seed(1998)
  as.data.frame(bootstrap_mean_ci(x, B = 2000, method = method))
})
do.call(rbind, comparison)
```

Percentile uses type-7 quantiles; basic reflects these about the sample mean.
Normal uses estimated bootstrap bias correction and bootstrap SE. BCa delegates
to `boot::boot.ci`, whose interpolation convention differs from type-7 quantiles.
No ranking of these methods can be established from one observed sample.

## Numerical protection

```{r}
set.seed(1998)
tiny <- bootstrap_mean_ci((1:10) * 1e-200)
set.seed(1998)
ordinary <- bootstrap_mean_ci(1:10)
c(tiny_SE_in_original_units = tiny$bootstrap_se / 1e-200,
  ordinary_SE = ordinary$bootstrap_se)
```

Extreme magnitudes and large offsets use centered, scaled arithmetic.
Unrepresentable intervals produce an error. Scaling protects computation;
it does not change the statistical assumptions.

## Interpretation and limitations

A 95% confidence procedure aims to contain the fixed population mean in 95% of
repeated samples under its assumptions. This is not a 95% probability statement
about the fixed mean after observing this particular interval. For the simulated
example we can check this interval's inclusion, but one result cannot establish
coverage:

```{r}
bootstrap$lower <= 2 && 2 <= bootstrap$upper
```

The authors' 10,000-dataset stress studies found substantial BCa undercoverage
and percentile undercoverage for scaled t(3) and contaminated normal data at
sample sizes 30 and 100. See the README for the reported results. Finite variance
alone does not guarantee BCa higher-order accuracy. The mean remains sensitive
to outliers, and ordinary resampling is inappropriate for clustered or dependent
data without a suitable design.

Constant observations produce a zero-width empirical bootstrap interval; this
is not evidence of zero population uncertainty. The t function rejects constant
samples. Bootstrap results report degeneracy and scaling diagnostics. Retained
warnings should be inspected rather than suppressed in routine analysis.

## Empirical coverage and reliability

A confidence interval that is computed successfully does not
necessarily achieve its nominal coverage probability. Bootstrap
performance depends on the population distribution, sample size,
and interval construction.

### Simulation design

A reproducible Monte Carlo study compared the BCa bootstrap
interval with the classical Student t interval.

- Random seed: 1998
- Confidence level: 95%
- Independent datasets: 1,000 per configuration
- Bootstrap resamples per dataset: 1,999
- Sample sizes: 20 and 50
- Populations: Exponential(rate = 1) and Student t(df = 3)

The population means were 1 and 0, respectively. Both intervals
were evaluated on the same simulated datasets.

### Empirical coverage

| Population | Sample size | BCa coverage | Student t coverage |
|:-----------|------------:|-------------:|-------------------:|
| Exponential(1) | 20 | 90.6% | 91.3% |
| Exponential(1) | 50 | 92.6% | 93.2% |
| Student t(3) | 20 | 89.5% | 96.2% |
| Student t(3) | 50 | 91.4% | 95.0% |

All 4,000 BCa intervals were computed successfully, with no
warnings in this experiment.

The BCa coverage estimates had Monte Carlo standard errors
of approximately 0.0083 to 0.0097. These quantify simulation
uncertainty, not uncertainty in individual confidence intervals.

### Paired comparison

The estimated BCa-minus-t coverage differences were:

| Population | Sample size | Difference | Paired MCSE |
|:-----------|------------:|-----------:|------------:|
| Exponential(1) | 20 | -0.007 | 0.0066 |
| Exponential(1) | 50 | -0.006 | 0.0057 |
| Student t(3) | 20 | -0.067 | 0.0080 |
| Student t(3) | 50 | -0.036 | 0.0062 |

The heavy-tailed settings showed substantially lower BCa
coverage than the classical t benchmark in this experiment.
These findings do not establish that one method is universally
preferable.

### Numerical stability

An earlier paired diagnostic compared 399 and 1,999 bootstrap
resamples using 200 datasets per population at sample size 20.

Seven warnings concerning extreme order statistics occurred
with 399 resamples, compared with none at 1,999 resamples
in that diagnostic.

Increasing the number of bootstrap resamples can reduce
bootstrap Monte Carlo variability. It does not eliminate
sampling bias, guarantee nominal coverage, or correct
dependence and other violations of statistical assumptions.

The package retains its default of 2,000 resamples.
Users may specify a different value through the B argument.

### Reference implementation

The BCa calculation uses boot::boot() for resampling and
boot::boot.ci() for interval construction.

A separate numerical verification compared the package
wrapper directly with these functions using normal,
exponential, and Student t(3) samples. All three comparisons
reproduced the reference bootstrap replicates and interval
endpoints to numerical tolerance.

This establishes agreement with the reference implementation
for the tested inputs, not universal coverage validity.

### Practical interpretation

- Inspect the distribution and dependence structure of the data.
- Do not interpret successful interval computation as proof
  of correct coverage.
- Treat extreme-order-statistic warnings as useful diagnostics.
- Use larger bootstrap resample counts when Monte Carlo
  stability is important.
- Consider sensitivity analyses when samples are small,
  highly skewed, or heavy-tailed.

The earlier validation study described in the package
documentation remains separate from this experiment.
